strengths: Comprehensive and thorough empirical study: the paper evaluates across long video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding benchmarks, with extensive ablations (branch combinations, information scaling, attention budget scaling), gate/branch analysis, and attention sink analysis both in the main text and a very detailed appendix.

The hybrid modality-aware design (dense GQA for text tokens, learnable NSA for video tokens) is sensible and well-motivated, and the paper is among the first to natively train NSA in a video-language model with end-to-end training on 216K video QA pairs.

The scaling analyses (information budget under fixed context, attention allocation at fixed budget, extrapolation to 128K from 36K training length) provide genuinely useful and reusable insights for practitioners designing efficient video LLMs.

Includes a fair competitive baseline: the authors fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-7B on the same training data (Dense-SFT) to disentangle gains from data adaptation versus the sparse attention mechanism (Table 3).

The analysis of branch-specific behaviors (compression dominance, selection/slide-window decay in deeper layers, task-dependent gating, branch-specific attention sink signatures) is an interesting contribution beyond raw benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is a direct adaptation of NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) to video tokens with a modality split; the architectural contribution is incremental and the paper does not introduce new technical mechanisms beyond applying an existing method with per-modality routing.

Results are 'competitive' rather than clearly superior: in Table 1, VideoNSA trails or merely matches training-free sparse baselines on several benchmarks (e.g., MInference ties on LongTimeScope at 44.4, XAttention beats VideoNSA on VSIBench 36.6 vs 36.1), and no variance/significance testing is reported, so many deltas appear within noise. The claim that VideoNSA 'consistently outperforms existing methods' is stronger than the evidence.

Missing an important baseline class: trainable sparse attention methods (e.g., SeerAttention) and a trainable-sparse video LLM comparison; training-free baselines are at a natural disadvantage when compared against a method with 4600 H100 GPU hours of training.

Efficiency claims are under-supported: while '3.6% of the attention budget' is highlighted, the paper's own Finding 5 shows the compression branch dominates runtime, and no end-to-end wall-clock latency, throughput, or memory comparison against the dense FlashAttention baseline across context lengths is provided. The efficiency story is therefore incomplete.

Writing and consistency issues undermine polish: the abstract lists four findings while the introduction lists six; training context length is stated as 36K in the main text but 32K in Appendix I; numerous typos ('imrpove', 'defination', 'similarites', 'meterial', 'Tavke', 'Iiterature'); project page/code/model links are empty in the abstract, hurting reproducibility claims.

Several result tables appear to contain errors: tri-shape and MInference rows are identical in Table 8, NSA-SLC and NSA-SWA rows are identical in Table 16, and Table 27 is labeled MLVU but lists Tomato subtask columns. These inconsistencies raise concerns about the reliability of the results pipeline.

No analysis of failure cases or of why gains on LongVideoBench are modest, and the dense-attention transfer result (Finding 1) shows the effect is 'limited' on one of the main benchmarks, which is not thoroughly explained.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper evaluates across six benchmarks (long-video, temporal, spatial) and includes an unusually detailed set of analyses (branch ablations, information-scaling studies up to 128K tokens, attention-budget allocation, gate/layer analysis, attention-sink analysis), which is more thorough than many efficiency papers.

The hybrid modality-split design (dense GQA for text tokens, learnable NSA for vision tokens) is a sensible and clearly motivated adaptation, and preserving text-token dense attention is a practical design choice for instruction-following.

The Dense-NSA vs. VideoNSA transfer experiment (Table 3) is an interesting probe of whether sparse-trained weights provide an inductive bias, and the training recipe/backbone details (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, 216K pairs, 4600 H100 hours) are mostly reported.
Evaluation against both token-compression and training-free sparse-attention baselines, plus a fair same-data SFT baseline, is appropriate experimental hygiene.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core contribution is applying the existing NSA mechanism (Yuan et al., 2025) to video tokens with a per-modality split and learned gates. The gating is a straightforward two-layer MLP and the architectural delta over prior work is small; the paper reads more as an empirical adaptation report than a methodological advance.

Results are incremental, not clearly superior: on LongVideoBench (60.0) and MLVU (51.8) VideoNSA essentially matches MInference/XAttention and does not beat non-sparse models like Video-XL-2 (61.0/52.2); on TimeScope the dense baseline is already 81.0 vs. 83.7. Only Tomato (+3~4) and VSIBench show clearer gains, and even there the margin over MInference is small (36.1 vs 36.5 on VSIBench, where a training-free method is better).

Missing efficiency evidence: despite being framed as a hardware-aware efficiency method, there is no end-to-end wall-clock, throughput, FLOPs, or memory comparison against the training-free sparse baselines; the only efficiency analysis (Finding 5) shows the method's own compression branch is the bottleneck, undercutting the efficiency narrative. The '3.6% of attention budget' claim is about computed edges, not measured speedup.

Quality-control problems suggest rushed preparation: the project page, code, and model links in the abstract are empty (contradicting the reproducibility statement); Table 27 is labeled 'MLVU' but reports Tomato subtask metrics; Tables 27/28 contain essentially duplicated rows; Figure 14 duplicates Figure 2; Table 3's VideoNSA LVB score (59.4) is inconsistent with Table 1 (60.0); references are duplicated (Pai et al. 2025a/b, Qin et al. 2025a/b, Zhang et al. 2024c/d); numerous typos ('Tavke 13', 'VideoNSAachieves', 'defination', 'capbility', 'imrpove'), and both Sections I and J refer to 'Figure 15' for different figures.

The claims in the abstract and conclusion ('significantly advances video understanding', 'consistently outperforms existing methods') are stronger than the evidence; on roughly half the benchmarks the method is at parity with or behind training-free baselines, and the long-video understanding results are described as only 'competitive' in the text.

Several key experimental details are unclear: it is ambiguous whether the single- and two-branch models in the ablation were trained from scratch or masked at test time; how the vision/text token split interacts with cross-attention (text queries attending to video tokens) is not precisely specified; statistical significance or multiple-run variance is not reported anywhere.

Training only on 350–550 frame videos (roughly 1.5–2.3 minutes at 4fps) while claiming scaling to 128K/10-hour videos raises distribution-shift questions that the paper acknowledges only implicitly, and the generalization claim rests on benchmarks whose videos may not match the claimed durations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: scaling video context length in VLMs, and provides what appears to be the first end-to-end trained, hardware-aware learnable sparse attention (NSA) applied to the video modality with a hybrid dense-text/sparse-video design.

The evaluation is broad, covering long video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial reasoning benchmarks, and includes a fair SFT baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B fine-tuned on the same data) to isolate the effect of sparse attention training.

VideoNSA achieves consistent improvements over the dense baseline on most benchmarks (e.g., Tomato +3.9, VSIBench +6.4, LongTimeScope +3.7) while using only ~3.6% of the full attention budget, and it improves over most training-free compression and sparse attention baselines.

The analysis section is unusually thorough: information-scaling and attention-budget studies (Figures 2-3), layer-wise and inter-head gate analysis, latency decomposition per branch (Figure 6), and a novel study of attention-sink formation across branches (Figures 7-9), yielding several interesting findings beyond raw benchmark numbers.
The extensive appendices (subtask results, branch-combination ablations, training hyperparameters, evaluation settings) support the claims and reproducibility of the training recipe.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core mechanism is directly adopted from NSA (Yuan et al., 2025b) with block size tied to frame token counts; the main contribution is the application/tuning to video plus empirical analysis, which may be considered incremental for a top-tier venue.

Efficiency claims are under-supported: despite 'hardware-aware' being central to the pitch, the paper provides no end-to-end wall-clock speedup, throughput, or memory comparison against dense FlashAttention or against the sparse/compression baselines. Finding 5 even concedes the compression branch is a major bottleneck, so the practical efficiency benefit is not clearly demonstrated.

Gains over the dense baseline are modest on several benchmarks (LVB +1.3, MLVU +0.6) and dense training-free methods (e.g., XAttention) already match or exceed VideoNSA on some tasks (e.g., XAttention 36.6 vs 36.1 on VSIBench), while stronger trained models (Video-XL-2) still lead on LVB/MLVU.

There are internal inconsistencies and signs of careless assembly: Table 1 reports VideoNSA LVB at 60.0 while Appendix Table 7 reports 60.2; Table 27 is labeled 'MLVU' but contains Tomato subtask columns; Tables 9 and 14 largely duplicate rows; text refers to 'Figure 15' for two different studies; typos ('imrpove', 'Tavke 13', 'meterial', 'capbility') appear throughout.
The project page, code, and model links in the abstract are empty, and given the 4600 H100-hour training cost, reproducibility and independent verification are currently limited.

Several analyses report only single runs/point estimates without variance or significance testing (e.g., Table 2 ablations where differences across branch subsets are small relative to benchmark noise, especially on Tomato and VSIBench).

Training data is filtered to 350-550 frame videos, restricting evaluation to long videos; the paper does not evaluate whether the sparse design degrades short-video or image understanding, which is important for a general video-language model.

strengths: First systematic adaptation of Native Sparse Attention (NSA) to video-language models with end-to-end training, introducing a sensible hybrid design (dense/GQA attention for text, learnable sparse attention for video tokens), and demonstrating scaling to 128K vision context with only ~3.6% of the full attention budget.

Very thorough experimental setup: comparisons against token compression, training-free sparse attention, quantization, and a matched SFT baseline on the same data, across six+ benchmarks (long video, temporal reasoning, spatial understanding) plus additional LSDBench and VideoEvalPro results, using standard evaluation toolkits.

Rich and unusually deep analysis: branch ablations, information-scaling and attention-budget scaling studies, layer-wise and inter-head gate analysis, attention sink quantification across branches, latency profiling identifying the compression branch/kernel as the bottleneck, and a theoretical appendix (routing-path stability, RoPE phase aliasing) that attempts to explain observed scaling behavior.

Useful empirical findings with practical value, e.g., learned sparse weights transferring partially to dense inference, optimal global–local allocation being task-dependent, and benchmark-specific routing strategies confirmed via PCA clustering and static-gate ablations.
Reproducibility efforts are reasonable: full hyperparameter tables, evaluation settings, and a stated intent to release code/model; training cost (4600 H100 GPU hours) is disclosed.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core mechanism is a direct application of NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) to video tokens with a modality split; the architectural contribution (block size = tokens per frame, modality-wise attention routing, sigmoid-gated branches) is relatively incremental. The paper is strongest as an empirical/systematic study rather than a new method.

Gains over strong training-free sparse baselines are modest and inconsistent: on LVB (60.0 vs Video-XL-2 61.0), MLVU (51.8 vs 52.2), and LongTimeScope (ties MInference at 44.4), VideoNSA is roughly competitive rather than clearly better; the clearest win is Tomato (26.5 vs 23.7). No variance/seeds or significance tests are reported for these small margins.

Evidence of sloppiness and internal inconsistencies undermines confidence: typos throughout (e.g., 'imrpove', 'capbility', 'defination', 'meterial', 'Tavke'); empty Project page/Code/Model fields; VideoNSA reported as 60.0 (Table 1/7) but 59.4 (Table 3/34); Table 31 is labeled MLVU but lists Tomato subtasks and duplicates rows from Table 32; NSA-SLC and NSA-SWA rows are numerically identical in Tables 2 and 18, which looks like a copy-paste error or a suspicious coincidence.

Efficiency claims are weaker than the framing suggests: training speedup is only 0.87x over dense; realized FLOPs are 0.56x (vs 0.24x ideal) due to kernel/head-padding limitations; the paper itself admits the compression branch is the dominant latency bottleneck; and decode-time/KV-cache memory benefits (the other half of long-video efficiency) are barely analyzed since text uses standard GQA and video KV cache is retained.

The 'four findings' in the abstract do not match the six findings in the introduction; several findings (e.g., task-dependent branch usage, dynamic attention sinks) are largely observational and their downstream utility is not clearly connected to actionable design recommendations.

Training data is a narrow filtered subset (videos with 350-550 frames at 4 fps), raising questions about generalization to other frame-length regimes; no evaluation of instruction-following or image benchmarks to verify the text branch's dense attention preserves general capabilities.

The theoretical appendix (routing-path stability, RoPE arguments) is informal and post-hoc; equations are mostly restatements without quantitative predictions that could be falsified against the experiments.

strengths: First attempt (to my knowledge) at natively trainable, hardware-aware sparse attention (NSA) for video-language models with hybrid modality-specific attention (NSA for vision, dense GQA for text), which is a sensible and well-motivated design direction.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six benchmarks (LongVideoBench, MLVU, TimeScope, LongTimeScope, Tomato, VSIBench) plus two additional ones, with a large set of training-free compression and sparse-attention baselines.

Substantial analysis effort: branch ablations, context-length and attention-budget scaling studies, gate-weight analysis across layers and heads, attention-sink analysis, latency profiling of each branch, and a RoPE/routing-path theoretical discussion in the appendix.

Interesting negative-space findings, e.g., the compression branch emerging as the latency bottleneck, task-dependent global–local allocation, and the observation that training-time allocation matters more than raw budget.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core technique is directly borrowed from Native Sparse Attention (Yuan et al., 2025c) with minimal architectural modification (modality split + GQA for text). The contribution is essentially an application/fine-tuning study rather than a new method, and the claimed design contributions (hybrid branches, dynamic gating) all come from NSA itself.

Headline results are weak for the claimed contribution: on LongVideoBench (60.0 vs 58.7), MLVU (51.8 vs 51.2), and TimeScope, gains over the untrained dense Qwen2.5-VL-7B are within noise, and training-free MInference matches or nearly matches VideoNSA on LongTimeScope (44.4 vs 44.4) and Tomato is the only clear win (26.5 vs ~23). 'Competitive' and 'narrowing the gap' (the authors' own words) is not convincing evidence that trainable sparse attention is preferable to training-free sparsity at 4600 H100 GPU hours of cost.

Efficiency claims are undermined by the paper's own measurements: actual FLOPs are 4.68 PF (0.56x) vs the ideal 0.24x due to query-head padding, prefill latency at short contexts (4k–16k) is worse than dense attention (0.2x–0.5x speedup in Figure 26b), and the compression branch dominates runtime. The paper effectively concedes the mechanism is not yet practical, which weakens the central 'efficiency + scalability' narrative.

Single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), single training dataset (a filtered subset of LLaVA-Video-178K), and the SFT baseline trained on the same data performs worse than the original dense model on several benchmarks, raising questions about training-data quality and whether the observed gains reflect sparse attention or general fine-tuning noise.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: VideoNSA's LongVideoBench score is reported as 60.0 (Table 1), 60.2 (Table 7), and 59.4 (Tables 3/34) without clear reconciliation; Table 31 and Table 32 contain identical numbers; typos and incomplete sentences (e.g., 'imrpove', 'capbility', unfinished sentence in the abstract, blank project page/code/model links), which suggests the submission was not carefully polished.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix M is largely hand-wavy: informal definitions of routing-path stability, no quantitative validation of Delta_i, and invoked results (LM-Infinite logit growth, RoPE phase aliasing) are not connected to specific measurements of the model.

The 'reliable scaling to 128K' claim is weakly supported: Table 27 shows MLVU drops from 51.8 (64k) to 48.7 (128k) and LTS drops from 44.4 to 42.9, so scaling is not uniformly reliable, and only two of five benchmarks improve at 128k.

No comparison against other trained/efficient long-video models (Video-XL-2 outperforms VideoNSA on LVB and MLVU), and no analysis of failure modes or statistical significance given that most deltas are 1-2 points.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: scaling video context length in video LLMs, where token compression has known limitations on reasoning-heavy tasks.

End-to-end training of a 7B model (4600 H100 GPU hours) with a hardware-aware sparse attention mechanism applied to video tokens is a substantial engineering effort, and the hybrid design (dense/GQA for text, NSA for video) is sensible and clearly motivated.

The evaluation is broad: 8+ benchmarks spanning long video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial reasoning, with both training-free sparse attention and token compression baselines, plus a fine-tuned dense baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-SFT) to isolate the effect of sparse training.

The analysis is unusually thorough: ablations over branch combinations, context-length and attention-budget scaling studies, gate/inter-head similarity analysis, latency profiling, attention-sink analysis, and a theoretical appendix relating scaling behavior to routing-path stability and RoPE geometry. The finding that sparse-trained weights transfer beneficially to dense inference (Dense-NSA) is interesting.

VideoNSA shows clear gains over the dense baseline on several tasks (e.g., Tomato, LongTimeScope, VSIBench) and runs with only ~3.6% of the attention budget, with results that are competitive with or better than strong training-free sparse baselines.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core mechanism is a direct application of Native Sparse Attention (Yuan et al., 2025) to video tokens with a modality-wise hybrid split. The main contribution is empirical adaptation and analysis rather than a new technique, and the block-size-per-frame design choice is straightforward.

Headline claims of 'significantly advances' and 'consistently outperforms existing methods' are stronger than the evidence: on several benchmarks VideoNSA only ties (MInference on LongTimeScope, 44.4) or trails (XAttention 36.6 vs 36.1 on VSIBench) the best training-free baselines, and specialized models like Video-XL-2 remain higher on LVB/MLVU. 'Competitive' is the accurate term, as the paper itself concedes in places.

The efficiency story is weaker than claimed in practice: theoretical FLOPs advantage (0.24x) degrades to 0.56x due to query-head padding, the compression branch becomes a latency bottleneck, and at short-to-mid contexts VideoNSA is slower than several baselines (Figure 26). No end-to-end decoding/memory analysis is given.

Evaluation is confined to a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) and a single training dataset (a 216K subset of LLaVA-Video-178K); generalization of the hybrid design across backbones, model scales, and data mixtures is not demonstrated.

There are inconsistencies and presentation issues: the abstract/main text reports Tomato = 26.5 while Table 3 reports 26.2; Tables 31/32 appear to contain duplicated rows with mismatched column headers (MLVU-labeled table with Tomato-like columns); some tables have '–' entries and a fully-collapsed 0.0 configuration (block count 4) suggesting fragile behavior at extreme allocations; typos and empty project/code/model links undermine the reproducibility statement.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix M is informal (prose-level appeals to routing stability and RoPE phase aliasing) rather than a rigorous result, and some notation in Section 2 (Eq. 2, indices) contains errors.
